label: copy-phase input e fed back early in the copy (recall_idx 1-3, t<=9)
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase when the fed-back input token is e (100% of activation mass on in_tok=e; never in the original or delimiter phases, and never on e as an original input). Restricted to early copy positions: recall_idx 1 (e was the first original token, input right after <DEL>) carries ~75% of mass and all the top activations (~4.7); recall_idx 2 ~21%, recall_idx 3 ~5%, essentially none beyond. Activation also fades with absolute step: dead after t~10, so e fed back late in long sequences (L>=7) does not fire. Magnitude is highest when e is the first copied token in short sequences (L=4-5); third-quartile examples (~1.5) are e at recall_idx 2. Does not depend on the token being output or neighbouring tokens. Rare tiny activations on g/x/s fed back right after <DEL>.

issues: Most of the factual claims hold up on dev. Activations appear only in the copy phase (share 1.000; 0 actives in the original and delimiter phases). in_tok=e carries 1.000 of the mass. There are no actives with in_first=1, so the feature never fires on e as an original input. By recall_idx the mass shares are 1: 0.746, 2: 0.208, 3: 0.046, 4: 6 steps. Firing has stopped by t=12 (t=10: 704 actives, t=11: 30). By L, the mass peaks at L=4-5. It does not depend on out_tok or next_out (flat lift of about 2x). Non-e copy inputs score precision 2e-5 and hold 0.016% of the mass.

The 'recall_idx <= 3' clause adds nothing. Given t<=8 it is redundant, and the t<=8 predicate with and without it scores the same test values (P 0.926, R 0.841, F1 0.881). The real control variable is absolute step t, or roughly recall_idx + t, which is the same as 2*recall_idx + L.

The predicate has one systematic false-positive class: copy-phase e at the t=9 boundary. Precision of copy-phase e by step is t=5 0.96, t=6 1.00, t=7 0.94, t=8 0.84, t=9 0.32, t=10 0.06. So 'up to t<=9' overclaims, because two thirds of copy-phase e inputs at t=9 do not fire. Within cells: r=1 L=8 (t=9) has precision 0.65, r=2 L=7 (t=9) 0.43, r=3 L=5 (t=8) 0.59, r=3 L=6 (t=9) 0.19.

I looked for a second variable behind the boundary cases (r=1, L=8) and found none. n_digits, in_count, a digit as the next token, and a vowel as first token all give precision 0.62-0.75. The edge is a graded decay with step, not a hidden condition. Alternative predicates move test F1 only a little: t<=8 gives 0.881, recall_idx+t<=10 gives 0.887 (P 0.931, R 0.848, mass 0.967), and the original gives 0.875. The explanation already says the feature dies out by step, so I am upholding it, with the boundary noted as soft.
